methodology.title: STRATA FitScore methodology
methodology.summary: FitScore is a transparent editorial shortlist for hypertrophy-oriented exercise selection. It is not a validated scientific instrument, a prediction of individual results, or a substitute for qualified coaching or medical care.
methodology.formula: A weighted five-factor baseline is calculated, then a small disclosed editorial adjustment accounts for exercise-specific trade-offs that the five fields do not fully represent. The published score is never changed by community ratings.

factors.label: Target stimulus
factors.description: How directly the movement can load the intended muscle when performed with appropriate technique.
factors.boundary: This is an editorial judgment informed by anatomy, mechanics, and exercise literature; it is not a direct measurement of muscle growth.

factors.label: Effective range
factors.description: Whether the movement can challenge the target through a useful and tolerable range of motion.
factors.boundary: More range is not automatically better for every person or exercise.

factors.label: Stability
factors.description: How readily effort can be directed to the target before balance or unrelated coordination becomes limiting.
factors.boundary: Stability is task-specific and does not mean that free-weight exercises are ineffective.

factors.label: Progression potential
factors.description: How easily load, repetitions, range, or technique can be measured and progressed over time.
factors.boundary: Progress still depends on consistent training and appropriate programming.

factors.label: Fatigue efficiency
factors.description: The expected target stimulus relative to non-target fatigue, setup burden, and recovery cost.
factors.boundary: Fatigue response is individual and varies with load, volume, and execution.

methodology.adjustment: Editorial adjustment is the difference between the weighted baseline and the published FitScore. It is shown explicitly and is capped to a small range in the current dataset. It captures setup, practicality, resistance-profile, and exercise-specific considerations without pretending those judgments are measured with scientific precision.
methodology.evidenceNote: Research supports broad training principles more strongly than exact head-to-head rankings of individual exercises. Every exercise page labels STRATA interpretation separately from the linked evidence.

sources.title: Which ROMs Lead to Rome? A Systematic Review of the Effects of Range of Motion on Muscle Hypertrophy
sources.publisher: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research / PubMed
sources.supports: The effective-range factor and the general relevance of training at longer muscle lengths.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not validate a specific STRATA score or prove that the exercise with the largest possible range is always superior.

sources.title: Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations
sources.publisher: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports / PubMed
sources.supports: The role of range of motion in strength and hypertrophy adaptations.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not establish one universally optimal range for every joint, person, or exercise.

sources.type: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis
sources.title: Resistance training prescription for muscle strength and hypertrophy in healthy adults
sources.publisher: British Journal of Sports Medicine / PubMed
sources.supports: Broad resistance-training prescription and the importance of progressive, repeated loading.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not provide exact scores for individual exercises.

sources.title: Machines and free weight exercises: comparing changes in muscle size, strength, and power
sources.publisher: Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness / PubMed
sources.supports: The conclusion that both machine and free-weight training can be effective, with strength adaptations showing task specificity.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not make every machine or free-weight variation equivalent.

sources.title: Resistance Training Load Effects on Muscle Hypertrophy and Strength Gain
sources.publisher: Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise / PubMed
sources.supports: The use of multiple loading ranges for hypertrophy and heavier loading for maximal-strength specificity.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not determine which exercise is best for a particular user.

sources.title: Progression Models in Resistance Training for Healthy Adults
sources.supports: The progression factor and general resistance-training progression principles.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not validate STRATA's exact weighting or exercise order.

sources.title: Anatomy and Physiology 2e: The Muscular System
sources.supports: Anatomical terminology and broad muscle actions used in target labels.
sources.doesNotSupport: Anatomy alone cannot establish comparative hypertrophy outcomes.

sources.title: ACE Exercise Library
sources.supports: General movement setup and execution context.
sources.doesNotSupport: It does not validate STRATA scores or personalized rankings.
